# WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021 update) — recommended AQG levels for SO2 (24-hour) and NO2 (annual)

## 1. Answer

| Pollutant | Averaging period | Recommended AQG level (final guideline value) |
|---|---|---|
| Sulfur dioxide (SO₂) | 24-hour mean | **40 µg/m³** |
| Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) | Annual mean | **10 µg/m³** |

These are the *final* AQG levels from the 2021 update — not interim targets. They are the values WHO recommends as the ultimate, health-based target for jurisdictions setting legally binding air quality standards.

For completeness of the same pollutant table (do not confuse with the two answers above):

- SO₂ also has a **10-minute mean** AQG of **500 µg/m³** (peak/short-term exposure). WHO 2021 sets **no annual** AQG for SO₂.
- NO₂ also has a **24-hour mean** AQG of **25 µg/m³** (short-term exposure).

## 2. Source of record and verification path

The values above are taken from the WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines: Particulate matter (PM₂.₅ and PM₁₀), ozone, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide and carbon monoxide. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2021 (ISBN 978-92-4-003422-8; https://apps.who.int/iris/handle/10665/345329; CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO).

Verbatim grounding, from the WHO IRIS copy of the guidelines' pollutant summary table (fetched by the research harness, sha256 2371e5cb9e22):

> "NO2 (nitrogen dioxide) ... Annual average 10 µg/m3 / 24-hour average 25 µg/m3"
>
> "SO2 (sulfur dioxide) ... 24-hour average 40 µg/m3 / 10-minute average 500 µg/m3"

Supporting statements from the WHO Q&A page "WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines" (22 September 2021):

> "The updated WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (AQGs) provide recommendations on air quality guideline levels as well as interim targets for six key air pollutants."
>
> "The AQG levels provide evidence-informed quantitative recommendations ... for PM₂.₅, PM₁₀, NO₂, O₃, SO₂ and CO, for relevant averaging times ..."
>
> "Annual and peak season is long-term exposure, while 24 hour and 8 hour is short-term exposure."

To re-verify independently, the authoritative location is the guideline's own summary-of-recommendations table (Chapter 3, Table 3.1 / the per-pollutant recommendation tables in the SO₂ and NO₂ sections), and the machine-readable IRIS record at handle 10665/345329.

## 3. AQG levels vs. interim targets (the most common error)

WHO 2021 publishes, for each pollutant/averaging period, a graded sequence of **interim targets (IT-1 … IT-n)** leading to the **AQG level**. The interim targets are progressively stricter, deliberately non-health-based milestones intended for regions whose current concentrations far exceed the guideline; the AQG level is the endpoint. The request asks for the *recommended AQG levels*, so only the final AQG values are reported here (40 µg/m³ for SO₂ 24-hour; 10 µg/m³ for NO₂ annual). The specific interim-target concentrations for these two pollutant/period pairs are not reproduced in this deliverable because they were not present in the verified source passages supplied; they should be read directly from the guideline tables rather than quoted from memory.

## 4. Statistical form and averaging conventions

Per the WHO Q&A footnote accompanying the 2021 table: "µg = microgram; ᵃ 99th percentile (i.e. 3–4 exceedance days per year)." The 24-hour AQG values (including SO₂ = 40 µg/m³) are specified as the **99th percentile of 24-hour means**, i.e. up to 3–4 exceedance days per year are tolerated in assessing compliance. The annual AQG (including NO₂ = 10 µg/m³) is a **long-term exposure** metric, assessed as the annual mean of 24-hour values.

## 5. Units

All values are reported in µg/m³, as requested and as WHO publishes them. For readers who need ppb (derived here by the standard conversion ppb = µg/m³ × 24.45 / molecular weight, at 25 °C and 101.325 kPa — these conversions are *not* WHO-published figures and carry rounding error):

- SO₂, 40 µg/m³ × 24.45 / 64.07 ≈ **15 ppb** (24-hour mean)
- NO₂, 10 µg/m³ × 24.45 / 46.01 ≈ **5 ppb** (annual mean)

## 6. Scope notes

- The figures refer to the **2021** update, not the 2005 WHO air quality guidelines (which set a different, less stringent SO₂ 24-hour value of 125 µg/m³ and NO₂ annual value of 40 µg/m³ — cited here only to prevent version confusion, not as an answer).
- Both are *ambient (outdoor) air* guideline levels; WHO 2021 does not issue indoor air quality guidelines in this document.
- The 2021 update also introduces new AQG levels not present in 2005 (e.g. 24-hour NO₂ and CO, peak-season O₃) and good practice statements for black carbon/elemental carbon, ultrafine particles, and sand-and-dust-storm particles, for which no numerical AQG could be derived.

question: X18
answer:
AES-GCM OPERATING LIMITS UNDER NIST SP 800-38D (Nov 2007), RBG-BASED IV CONSTRUCTION

SOURCES AND SCOPE
Primary text: NIST SP 800-38D, 'Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation: Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) and GMAC', M. Dworkin, November 2007 (https://tsapps.nist.gov/publication/get_pdf.cfm?pub_id=51288, sha256 2ffac947dbe5...). Corroborating: the 2021 public-comment compilation on SP 800-38D (sp800-38d-initial-public-comments-2021.pdf), which restates the same Section 8.3 limit and its single exemption. Note: the NIST *landing page* for the publication (nist.gov/publications/...) contains only bibliographic metadata and states none of the three figures; all three are in the PDF itself. Answers below are for the 2007 edition, not the later revision drafts.

Normative clauses used:
- Sec. 5.2.1.1 (input-length requirements; contains the len(P)/len(A)/len(IV) bullets and the 96-bit IV recommendation).
- Sec. 8.2.2 (RBG-based construction: random field + free field; r(i) >= 96 bits, fixed for the life of the key).
- Sec. 8.3 (constraints on the number of invocations).
- Appendix C, Tables 1 and 2 (tag-length-dependent packet constraints), relevant only when short tags are used.

=== ANSWER 1 - IV LENGTH IMPLEMENTATIONS SHOULD RESTRICT SUPPORT TO ===
96 bits (12 bytes).

Verbatim, Sec. 5.2.1.1: 'For IVs, it is recommended that implementations restrict support to the length of 96 bits, to promote interoperability, efficiency, and simplicity of design.'

Status: a RECOMMENDATION ('it is recommended'), not a shall. It is the interoperability default; it is not the set of legal IV lengths.

Legal envelope, for completeness, from the same input-length bullet list:
  1 <= len(IV) <= 2^64 - 1 bits.
Under the RBG-based construction specifically (Sec. 8.2.2), for each supported IV length i the split is IV = random_field || free_field, with:
  - r(i) = bit length of the random field, r(i) >= 96 bits, and r(i) fixed for the life of the key;
  - the free field may be empty (and is empty when the IV is exactly the random field);
  - the random field is either a direct random string of r(i) bits from an approved RBG of sufficient security strength, or the r(i)-bit incrementing-function successor of the preceding IV's random field under the same key;
  - for any supported IV length >= 96 bits, exactly one construction (deterministic Sec. 8.2.1 OR RBG Sec. 8.2.2) shall be used across all instances under a given key - not both.
Engineering guidance: support 96-bit IVs as the sole IV length in new designs (the 'restrict support to 96 bits' recommendation). If an implementation accepts other lengths, it must fix r(i) per length for the key's lifetime and must still honour the 2^32 cap in Answer 2.

=== ANSWER 2 - MAXIMUM TOTAL INVOCATIONS OF THE AUTHENTICATED ENCRYPTION FUNCTION UNDER ONE KEY ===
2^32 = 4,294,967,296 invocations, aggregated over ALL IV lengths and ALL instances of the authenticated encryption function that use the key.

Verbatim, Sec. 8.3: 'The total number of invocations of the authenticated encryption function shall not exceed 2^32, including all IV lengths and all instances of the authenticated encryption function with the given key.'

The single exemption in Sec. 8.3 does not apply here: the cap is lifted only if the implementation uses exclusively 96-bit IVs generated by the DETERMINISTIC construction (Sec. 8.2.1). The question fixes the RBG-based construction, so the 2^32 cap applies without exception. (Corroborated by the 2021 comments: 'the total number of invocations ... is limited to no more than 2^32, unless one uses only 96-bit IVs that are generated using the deterministic construction.')

This is a shall, and it is a per-key, system-wide counter: it spans every module/process/device sharing the key, so a per-process counter is necessary but not sufficient - the controlling system must partition keys so that no key is shared beyond a bounded number of writers.

=== ANSWER 3 - MAXIMUM PLAINTEXT LENGTH PER INVOCATION, IN BYTES ===
68,719,476,704 bytes = 2^36 - 32 bytes (= 2^39 - 256 bits = 64 GiB - 32 bytes).

Verbatim, Sec. 5.2.1.1: 'The bit lengths of the input strings to the authenticated encryption function shall meet the following requirements: len(P) <= 2^39 - 256; len(A) <= 2^64 - 1; 1 <= len(IV) <= 2^64 - 1.'

Working (byte conversion):
  2^39                = 549,755,813,888 bits
  minus 256           = 549,755,813,632 bits
  divide by 8         = 68,719,476,704 bytes
  exact?              yes - 2^39 - 256 is divisible by 8, since 2^39 is and 256 = 8 x 32
  closed form         = 2^36 - 32 bytes  (2^36 = 68,719,476,736; minus 32 = 68,719,476,704)
  round-trip check    = 68,719,476,704 x 8 = 549,755,813,632 = 2^39 - 256  (matches the spec bit bound exactly)
This limit is independent of the IV construction: it holds for the deterministic and RBG-based constructions alike, and it is a shall.

CAVEAT that reduces this figure when short tags are used (Appendix C): with 32-bit tags, Table 1 caps ciphertext+AAD per packet at 2^5 ... 2^10 bytes (paired with 2^22 ... 2^11 decryption invocations); with 64-bit tags, Table 2 caps it at 2^15 ... 2^25 bytes (paired with 2^32 ... 2^17 invocations). One row of the applicable table 'shall be enforced'. So 2^36 - 32 bytes is the unconditional ceiling only for full 128-bit tags; with 32- or 64-bit tags the effective per-invocation plaintext budget is the table row's combined ciphertext+AAD figure minus the AAD length. Full 128-bit tags: no table constraint, 2^36 - 32 bytes stands.

=== REFERENCE IMPLEMENTATION CONSTANTS AND ENFORCEMENT PROCEDURE ===
Constants (bit-accurate):
  IV_LEN_RECOMMENDED_BITS   = 96
  IV_LEN_RECOMMENDED_BYTES  = 12
  IV_RANDOM_FIELD_MIN_BITS  = 96        // Sec. 8.2.2, r(i) >= 96
  IV_LEN_MIN_BITS           = 1
  IV_LEN_MAX_BITS           = 2^64 - 1
  MAX_INVOCATIONS_PER_KEY   = 2^32       // = 4294967296, Sec. 8.3, all IV lengths, all instances
  MAX_PLAINTEXT_BITS        = 2^39 - 256 // = 549755813632
  MAX_PLAINTEXT_BYTES       = 68719476704 // = 2^36 - 32
  MAX_AAD_BITS              = 2^64 - 1
  TAG_BITS_FULL             = 128
  // Appendix C, when tag_len < 128:
  TABLE_1_32BIT_TAG = [(2^5, 2^22), (2^6, 2^20), (2^7, 2^18), (2^8, 2^15), (2^9, 2^13), (2^10, 2^11)]  // (max ciphertext+AAD bytes, max decryption invocations)
  TABLE_2_64BIT_TAG = [(2^15, 2^32), (2^17, 2^29), (2^19, 2^26), (2^21, 2^23), (2^23, 2^20), (2^25, 2^17)]

Encryption-path checks, in order:
  1. IV length: reject any len(IV) not in [1 bit, 2^64 - 1 bits]; if the module adopts the recommendation, accept exactly 96 bits and reject everything else with a distinct 'unsupported IV length' error (do not silently pad or truncate - padding a short IV changes GCM's counter derivation and breaks the uniqueness argument).
  2. RBG construction discipline: r(i) >= 96 bits and fixed for the key's lifetime; free field length fixed for the key's lifetime; never mix deterministic and RBG construction for the same IV length under one key.
  3. Plaintext length: reject len(P) > 2^39 - 256 bits, i.e. reject len(P_bytes) > 68,719,476,704. Reject before any counter block is produced, so no ciphertext is emitted for an over-length message.
  4. AAD length: reject len(A) > 2^64 - 1 bits.
  5. Short-tag path: if tag_len == 32, select one Table 1 row and enforce both the per-packet combined ciphertext+AAD byte cap and that row's decryption-invocation cap for the key; likewise Table 2 for tag_len == 64. Enforce the row, do not interpolate.
  6. Invocation counter: increment a durable per-key counter on every call to the authenticated encryption function, before returning the ciphertext; if the post-increment value would exceed 4,294,967,296, fail closed (return an error, emit no ciphertext) and rotate the key. Persist the counter so a power loss cannot reset it (Sec. 9.1 concern); the counter is per key, not per key-and-IV-length, because Sec. 8.3 aggregates across all IV lengths.
  7. Key partitioning: because no single module can enforce a system-wide count, the higher layer must bound how many writers share a key - e.g. give each writer its own key, or pre-allocate each key a slice of the 2^32 budget - so the sum across instances stays <= 2^32.

Pseudocode:
  def gcm_encrypt(key, iv, plaintext, aad, tag_len=128):
      if not (1 <= bitlen(iv) <= 2**64 - 1): raise UnsupportedIVLength
      if RECOMMEND_96_ONLY and bitlen(iv) != 96: raise UnsupportedIVLength
      if bitlen(plaintext) > 2**39 - 256: raise PlaintextTooLong        # > 68719476704 bytes
      if bitlen(aad) > 2**64 - 1: raise AADTooLong
      if tag_len in (32, 64):
          row = select_row(tag_len)                                     # fixed, documented choice
          if len(plaintext) + len(aad) > row.max_combined_bytes: raise PacketTooLong
          if decrypt_count[key] >= row.max_decryptions: raise KeyExhausted
      with key_lock(key):
          if encrypt_count[key] >= 2**32: raise KeyExhausted            # Sec. 8.3
          encrypt_count[key] += 1                                       # durable, pre-emit
      return core_gcm(key, iv, plaintext, aad, tag_len)

=== SUMMARY TABLE ===
  (1) IV length to restrict support to ....... 96 bits (12 bytes)  [recommended, Sec. 5.2.1.1]
  (2) Max invocations per key ................ 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 [shall, Sec. 8.3; no exemption under RBG construction]
  (3) Max plaintext per invocation ........... 2^39 - 256 bits = 2^36 - 32 bytes = 68,719,476,704 bytes [shall, Sec. 5.2.1.1; 128-bit tags]

=== ASSUMPTIONS (stated, not hidden) ===
- 2007 edition of SP 800-38D is authoritative for these figures; later drafts/comments are used only to corroborate the 2^32 reading.
- Byte figure for (3) is exact (no rounding): the bit bound is divisible by 8.
- Figure (3) is the unconditional per-invocation ceiling; where 32- or 64-bit tags are configured, the Appendix C table row is the binding, smaller limit.
- Section numbers cited (5.2.1.1, 8.2.2, 8.3, Appendix C) follow the 2007 edition's numbering; the quoted text is reproduced verbatim above so the figures can be verified independently of the numbering.

question: X26
answer:
WebAssembly 3.0 linear-memory limits: page size, i32 maximum, its byte equivalent, and the i64 maximum

== 1. Answers ==

| # | Question | Answer | Bytes equivalent |
|---|----------|--------|------------------|
| 1 | Page size | 65,536 bytes (2^16 B = 64 KiB) | 65,536 |
| 2 | Max pages a memory with address type i32 may declare | 65,536 pages (2^16) | 4,294,967,296 (4 GiB = 2^32) |
| 3 | That i32 maximum in bytes | 4,294,967,296 bytes = 4 GiB | 4,294,967,296 |
| 4 | Corresponding page limit for address type i64 (declared max field) | 137,438,953,471 pages (2^37 − 1) | 9,007,199,254,675,456 (2^53 − 2^16) |

Worked arithmetic
- 2^16 = 65,536 (page size in bytes).
- i32 pages: 2^16 = 65,536 pages.
- i32 bytes: 65,536 pages × 65,536 bytes/page = 2^16 × 2^16 = 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 bytes = 4 GiB.
- i64 pages (declared max): 2^37 − 1 = 137,438,953,472 − 1 = 137,438,953,471 pages.
- i64 bytes at that max: (2^37 − 1) × 2^16 = 2^53 − 2^16 = 9,007,199,254,740,992 − 65,536 = 9,007,199,254,675,456 bytes.

== 2. Provenance (quotations from the grounding) ==

Page size — WebAssembly Specification, Release 3.0, exec/runtime.html, “Memory Instances”:
  “The length of the sequence always is a multiple of the WebAssembly page size, which is defined to be the constant 65536 – abbreviated 64 Ki.”

32-bit and 64-bit declared maxima — WebAssembly JS Interface (js-api), “Implementation-defined Limits”:
  “The maximum min or max field of a 32-bit memory is 65,536 pages (4 GiB).”
  “The maximum min or max field of a 64-bit memory is 2^37-1 pages (2^53 - 2^16 bytes).”
  “The maximum size of a 32-bit memory is 65,536 pages (4 GiB).”
  “The maximum size of a 64-bit memory is 262,144 pages (16 GiB).”

Bytes-from-pages rule — js-api:
  “Let maxsize be the max value in memtype * 65536.”

Address types exist for memories — core spec appendix/changes.html (“64-bit Address Space”, citing the memory64 proposal):
  “Added the ability to declare an i32/i64 address type for tables and memories.” / “Memory types include an address type.”

Note on the supplied proof of absence: it covers only https://webassembly.github.io/spec/core/appendix/changes.html, which is the change-history page and legitimately contains none of “page size”, “64KiB”, “65536”, “bytes”, “page”. That page only records that a 64-bit address type was added. The page-size constant is stated in exec/runtime.html, so ask 1 is answered from the grounding and is not a “none stated” case.

== 3. Reading of the four asks ==

- “Declare at most” is read as the maximum value the memory type's limits field (min/max) may take — i.e. the value a module may put in the max (or min) field of a memory type, not an engine's current allocation.
- The max field is optional. When omitted, the type is unbounded within the address type's range, i.e. the effective ceiling is still the same limit (2^16 pages for i32, the i64 range bound below for i64).
- The i32 figure is the same in both places: the core validation range for i32 memory limits is 2^16 pages, and the standard JS embedding restates it as 65,536 pages (4 GiB).

== 4. Two scopes for the 64-bit number — do not conflate them ==

(a) Declared maximum under the standard WebAssembly JS embedding (the figure reported for ask 4):
    2^37 − 1 = 137,438,953,471 pages (= 2^53 − 2^16 bytes).
    Rationale of the bound: byte sizes must stay inside the range where a JS Number is an exact integer (≤ 2^53), and (2^37 − 1) × 2^16 = 2^53 − 2^16 is the largest page count whose byte size stays under 2^53.

(b) Pure core-validation bound for i64 memories (the language-level range of the limits field):
    2^48 pages = 281,474,976,710,656 pages = 2^64 bytes = 18,446,744,073,709,551,616 bytes.
    Derivation from stated parts: i64 addresses are 64 bits ⇒ address space 2^64 bytes; page size is 2^16 bytes ⇒ 2^64 / 2^16 = 2^48 pages. This mirrors the i32 case exactly (2^32 bytes / 2^16 = 2^16 pages).
    The JS API number (a) is stricter and is an embedding limit, not the core validation range; a conforming non-JS embedder may accept a declared max up to 2^48 pages.

(c) Runtime growth cap in the JS embedding (distinct from the declared max):
    “The maximum size of a 64-bit memory is 262,144 pages (16 GiB)” = 2^18 pages × 2^16 B = 2^34 bytes = 17,179,869,184 bytes = 16 GiB. A module may declare a max above this, but growth past 262,144 pages throws a RuntimeError in that embedding.

Ordering check (all consistent, nothing exceeds a stated threshold):
  2^16 pages (i32 declared max) = 65,536 pages
  < 2^18 pages (JS runtime growth cap for i64) = 262,144 pages
  < 2^37 − 1 pages (JS declared max for i64) = 137,438,953,471 pages
  < 2^48 pages (core validation range for i64) = 281,474,976,710,656 pages.
Byte sizes: 2^32 (4 GiB) < 2^34 (16 GiB) < 2^53 − 2^16 < 2^64.

== 5. Implementation checklist ==

1. Encode page size as the constant 65,536 (2^16); never hard-code 4096.
2. For a memory type with address type i32: reject (CompileError in the JS embedding) any min or max field > 65,536; byte size = pages × 65,536, and the maximum byte size 2^32 = 4 GiB is not representable in i32 (largest u32 is 2^32 − 1), so expose sizes in pages or in u64/i64.
3. For a memory type with address type i64: under the standard JS embedding reject min/max > 2^37 − 1 = 137,438,953,471 pages; under the pure core rules the ceiling is 2^48 pages = 2^64 bytes. Keep the two limits in separate code paths/config, since the embedding limit is a compile-time policy, not a language rule.
4. Cap runtime growth separately from the declared max (JS embedding: 262,144 pages = 16 GiB for 64-bit memories; 65,536 pages = 4 GiB for 32-bit memories), raising RuntimeError rather than CompileError.
5. Accept an absent max field and treat it as the address type's ceiling, not as zero or as an implementation-defined number.

COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION — Australian LIPD Class Licence, 'digital modulation' transmitters, 2400–2483.5 MHz, as at 17 November 2026

1. WHICH INSTRUMENT IS IN FORCE ON 17 NOVEMBER 2026

The governing instrument is the Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025 (Federal Register ID F2025L01047). From the as-made text:

  "Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025 ... Dated: 4 September 2025 ... Authorised Version F2025L01047 registered 05/09/2025"
  "1 Name — This instrument is the Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025."
  "2 Commencement — This instrument commences at the start of 1 October 2025."

Why not an earlier or later instrument:
- LIPD 2015 (F2015L01438): the register entry in the record shows "No longer in force", latest compilation "F2023C00524 C1019 May 2023 - 30 September 2025". Its currency ended the day before the 2025 instrument commenced.
- LIPD 2000 (F2005B00339): register entry shows "No longer in force" / repealed; the 2014 compilation (F2014C00930) is historical only.
- Nothing in the record shows any instrument made after F2025L01047, and 17 November 2026 is after its 1 October 2025 commencement. The 2025 instrument is therefore the one in force on the date asked about.
- The two NICTA (Papua New Guinea) PDFs in the source list are PNG national consultation documents, not Australian law, and are excluded from this determination.

2. ASK 2 — MAXIMUM EIRP FOR 'DIGITAL MODULATION' IN 2400–2483.5 MHz

Answer: 4 W EIRP.

Source: Schedule 1, Part 8 ("Frequency hopping, WiFi and RLAN transmitters"), Table 8, item 7, of F2025L01047. The table as fetched reads:

  "Item | Column 1 Class of radiocommunications transmitter | Column 2 Permitted operating frequency band | Column 3 Maximum EIRP | Column 4 Additional limitations
   ...
   7  Digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters  2400–2483.5 MHz  4 W  See clause 43
   8  Digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters  5150–5250 MHz  1 W, averaged over the entire transmission burst  See clause 44"

Column 3 is expressly headed "Maximum EIRP", so the 4 W figure is an EIRP limit, not a conducted transmitter-power limit. Item 7 is the only Table 8 entry for digital modulation in 2400–2483.5 MHz; the two 2400–2483.5 MHz frequency-hopping entries (items 2 and 3, 500 mW and 4 W) do not apply to digital modulation.

Unit conversions for the compliance file:
  4 W = 4000 mW
  10·log10(4000 mW / 1 mW) = 36.0 dBm
  So the limit is 4 W EIRP = 36 dBm EIRP.

Worked application (EIRP vs conducted power): the limit binds at the antenna, so permitted conducted power = 4 W ÷ (linear antenna gain). Examples: 0 dBi → 4 W (36 dBm) conducted; 6 dBi → 1.0 W (30 dBm); 10 dBi → 400 mW (26 dBm); 20 dBi → 40 mW (16 dBm). Any device whose conducted power plus antenna gain exceeds 36 dBm EIRP is outside the class licence for this item.

3. ASK 3 — ADDITIONAL LIMIT ON RADIATED PEAK POWER SPECTRAL DENSITY

Status: NOT DETERMINABLE FROM THE AVAILABLE RECORD — blocked, not answered.

What the record does establish: item 7's column 4 reads "See clause 43". The licence's interpretation provision confirms that column 4 is where such conditions live: "additional limitation, for a class of radiocommunications transmitters, means a limitation in a clause mentioned in column 4 of the table item in Schedule 1 for that class". So a clause-43 additional limitation exists as a matter of the instrument's structure, and it is a separate condition sitting on top of the 4 W EIRP cap, not an alternative to it.

What the record does not contain: the text of clause 43. The passages fetched from F2025L01047 include clauses 3 and 4 of the preliminary part, clause 38 ("No additional requirements apply to Table 8"), clause 3 ("Additional limitation for table item 23": 10 mW transmitter power; 13 dBm per 1 MHz radiated PSD) and clause 4 ("Additional limitations for table item 25": 10 dBm per 250 MHz; -48 dBm per 1 MHz above 30 degrees elevation) — but not clause 43. Clauses 39–42 and 44 are likewise only referenced, not quoted. Accordingly no figure, bandwidth or unit can be stated for the digital-modulation 2400–2483.5 MHz PSD condition without inventing it.

Two traps explicitly avoided:
(a) Do not carry forward the repealed LIPD 2000 value. The 2014 compilation of the 2000 licence shows item 45A "Digital modulation transmitters 2400–2483.5 4 W — 1. # AES-GCM with RBG-based IVs — normative parameters and enforcement profile

Source: M. Dworkin, *Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation: Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) and GMAC*, NIST SP 800-38D, November 2007 (DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-38D). Sections used: 5.2.1.1 (input lengths and IV recommendation), 8.2.2 (RBG-based IV construction), 8.3 (constraints on the number of invocations), Appendix C (authentication assurance).

**Text-extraction caveat (read this before transcribing anything).** The machine-readable text of the PDF loses superscripts. Two figures appear mangled and must be restored:

| As extracted | Actual | Where |
|---|---|---|
| `232` | 2^32 | §8.3 invocation cap |
| `239-256` | 2^39 − 256 | §5.2.1.1 plaintext bit limit |
| `264-1` | 2^64 − 1 | §5.2.1.1 AAD / IV ceilings |
| `2,*'` / `2,*` | 2^−32 | §8.3 IV-collision bound |

Restoration is confirmed by §8.3's own worked example (2^10 devices partitioned into 2^20 / 2^21 / 2^20 local limits, which only sums correctly under a 2^32 global cap) and by the SP 800-38D public-comment corpus, which quotes the same sentences with the exponents intact.

---

## 1. Parameter table (the answer)

| # | Parameter | Value | Normative basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Supported IV length | **96 bits = 12 bytes** | §5.2.1.1 (recommendation); §8.2.2 (random field ≥ 96 bits, free field may be empty) |
| 2 | Max total authenticated-encryption invocations per key | **2^32 = 4,294,967,296** | §8.3 |
| 3 | Max plaintext per invocation | **2^39 − 256 bits** | §5.2.1.1 |
| 4 | Max plaintext per invocation, in bytes | **2^36 − 32 = 68,719,476,704 bytes** | conversion of row 3 |
| — | Permitted IV range (not recommended support) | 1 ≤ len(IV) ≤ 2^64 − 1 bits | §5.2.1.1 |
| — | Max AAD per invocation | len(A) ≤ 2^64 − 1 bits | §5.2.1.1 |
| — | IV-collision probability bound | ≤ 2^−32 | §8.3 |

---

## 2. Ask 1 — IV length: 96 bits (12 bytes)

§5.2.1.1, verbatim: *"For IVs, it is recommended that implementations restrict support to the length of 96 bits, to promote interoperability, efficiency, and simplicity of design."*

This recommendation is independent of the IV construction: it applies identically to the deterministic and the RBG-based constructions. What changes under §8.2.2 is only the internal structure of the 96-bit string:

- §8.2.2: *"the IV is the concatenation of two fields, called the random field and the free field… the length of the random field shall be at least 96 bits; the free field may be empty."*
- Field lengths *"shall be fixed for the life of the key"* for each supported IV length.

**Profile decision:** support exactly one IV length, 96 bits, with r(i) = 96 and an **empty free field**. The IV is then precisely the 96-bit *direct random string* from an approved RBG of sufficient security strength, or a successor produced by the r(i)-bit incrementing function (§8.2.2). No deterministic field is appended, which is what distinguishes this from the deterministic construction.

Why restrict rather than accept the full 1…2^64−1 range:

- Interoperability: the standard's stated rationale; peers will send 12-byte nonces.
- Efficiency: a 96-bit IV is used directly as J0 = IV ‖ 0^31 ‖ 1, skipping the GHASH-based derivation applied to other lengths.
- Simplicity: one code path, one length check, one field layout, no per-length random-field bookkeeping.
- Security: it keeps the IV-collision analysis (§8.3, §8.2.2) at its most favourable point.

Note: restricting to 96 bits does **not** buy the §8.3 exemption. The exemption requires 96-bit IVs *from the deterministic construction*; this profile is RBG-based, so the 2^32 cap in §3 below binds unconditionally.

---

## 3. Ask 2 — invocations per key: 2^32 = 4,294,967,296

§8.3, verbatim (exponent restored): *"The total number of invocations of the authenticated encryption function shall not exceed 2^32, including all IV lengths and all instances of the authenticated encryption function with the given key."*

**Applicability.** §8.3 opens: *"The following requirement applies to all implementations that use either 1) the deterministic construction with IVs whose length is not 96, or 2) the RBG-based construction, for IVs of any length. In other words, unless an implementation only uses 96-bit IVs that are generated by the deterministic construction…"* This profile is case (2), so the cap is mandatory and the escape clause is unavailable.

**Scope of the count — three dimensions, all global:**

1. *All IV lengths* — irrelevant here (one length), but it forbids a design that treats a second IV length as a fresh budget.
2. *All instances* — every device, thread, process, writer, or node holding the same key draws from the same 2^32.
3. *Authenticated encryption only* — the 2^32 figure is a cap on the encryption function. Authenticated **decryption** attempts are a separate concern: Appendix C advises monitoring and, if necessary, limiting unsuccessful verification attempts per key, and the 32-bit/64-bit tag rows of Table 1/Table 2 impose much tighter combined ciphertext+AAD and decryption-invocation limits whenever t < 128.

The standard's own method for satisfying the global cap is *local* partitioning: *"suppose an implementation consists of 2^10 devices that only support 64-bit, 96-bit, and 128-bit IVs. One way to satisfy the above requirement would be to limit each device to 2^20 invocations with 64-bit IVs, 2^21 invocations with 96-bit IVs, and 2^20 invocations with 128-bit IVs."* A deployment must therefore publish a per-instance quota whose sum over all instances never exceeds 2^32.

**Consistency with the IV-collision bound.** §8.3 pairs the cap with the requirement that *"the probability that the authenticated encryption function ever will be invoked with the same IV and the same key on two (or more) distinct sets of input data shall be no greater than 2^−32."* For 96-bit random IVs and r invocations, the birthday bound gives

  P(collision) ≈ (r² / 2) / 2^96 = r² / 2^97.

At r = 2^32: 2^64 / 2^97 = **2^−33**, which satisfies ≤ 2^−32. At r = 2^33 it would be 2^−31 and violate the bound. The two numbers are therefore mutually calibrated — the 2^32 cap is the largest value that keeps a 96-bit random-IV implementation inside its collision budget, and it must not be raised.

---

## 4. Asks 3 and 4 — max plaintext per invocation, in bytes

§5.2.1.1, verbatim (exponents restored): *"The bit lengths of the input strings to the authenticated encryption function shall meet the following requirements: • len(P) ≤ 2^39 − 256; • len(A) ≤ 2^64 − 1; • 1 ≤ len(IV) ≤ 2^64 − 1."*

Derivation of the byte figure (ask 4):

```
len(P)max = 2^39 − 256 bits
          = (2^39 − 256) / 8 bytes        (both terms divisible by 8: 2^39/8 = 2^36, 256/8 = 32)
          = 2^36 − 32 bytes
          = 68,719,476,736 − 32
          = 68,719,476,704 bytes
```

Independent check through bits:

```
2^39            = 549,755,813,888
− 256           = 549,755,813,632 bits
/ 8             = 68,719,476,704 bytes   ✓
```

Equivalent expressions: **64 GiB − 32 bytes**; ≈ 68.72 GB decimal; ≈ 2^36 bytes.

Why the −256: the GCTR counter space is 32 blocks wide per invocation, and the last two blocks of the 2^32-block counter domain are reserved (J0 for the tag mask, and the block encoding the length of A and C). Usable counter blocks = 2^32 − 2, each 128 bits ⇒ (2^32 − 2) × 128 = 2^39 − 256 bits.

Boundary property worth noting in tests: 2^36 is a multiple of 16 and 32 is a multiple of 16, so the maximum plaintext is a whole number of AES blocks (4,294,967,296 blocks); there is no partial trailing block at the limit. AAD may be up to 2^64 − 1 bits (i.e. 2^61 − 1 whole bytes plus a partial byte).

---

## 5. Enforcement specification

### 5.1 Constants

```c
#include <stdint.h>

/* NIST SP 800-38D (Nov 2007) */
#define GCM_IV_BYTES          12u                       /* 96 bits            — §5.2.1.1 */
#define GCM_MAX_INVOCATIONS   (UINT64_C(1) << 32)       /* 4294967296         — §8.3     */
#define GCM_MAX_PT_BYTES      ((UINT64_C(1) << 36) - 32)/* 68719476704 bytes  — §5.2.1.1, converted */
#define GCM_MAX_AAD_BITS      UINT64_MAX                /* 2^64 - 1 bits      — §5.2.1.1 */
```

`GCM_MAX_INVOCATIONS` must be a 64-bit type: a 32-bit counter overflows to zero exactly at the limit and silently re-opens the budget.

### 5.2 Seal (authenticated encryption) — check order matters

```
seal(key_ctx, iv, pt, aad):
  1. if len(iv) != GCM_IV_BYTES                 -> ERR_BAD_IV_LENGTH
  2. if len(pt) >  GCM_MAX_PT_BYTES             -> ERR_PLAINTEXT_TOO_LONG
  3. if len(aad) > (GCM_MAX_AAD_BITS / 8)       -> ERR_AAD_TOO_LONG
  4. if key_ctx.invocations_used >= GCM_MAX_INVOCATIONS
                                                -> ERR_KEY_EXHAUSTED   (no ciphertext emitted)
  5. key_ctx.invocations_used += 1              (persist BEFORE releasing output)
  6. iv := RBG(96 bits)                          /* direct random string, empty free field, §8.2.2 */
  7. (C, T) := GCM_Encrypt(key, iv, pt, aad)     /* t = 128 assumed */
  8. return (iv, C, T)
```

Ordering rationale: steps 1–3 reject malformed input before any budget is consumed, so a caller cannot burn the invocation budget with invalid requests (availability/DoS consideration). Step 4 tests *before* incrementing, so exactly 2^32 invocations succeed and the 2^32+1-th fails.

### 5.3 Failure behaviour

- **Never** fall back from an RBG failure to a counter, timestamp, or truncated IV. §8.2.2 permits a successor produced by the r(i)-bit incrementing function only from a *direct random string* already drawn under the same key; it does not permit substituting a fresh non-random value. RBG failure ⇒ return an error and emit no ciphertext.
- On `ERR_KEY_EXHAUSTED`, the key must be retired, not reset. A monotonic per-key identifier must prevent a restarted process from reinitialising the counter to zero.
- Persistence: the counter must survive power loss without regressing (§8.2.2/§9.1 uniqueness obligations). Either write the counter durably before returning ciphertext, or pre-reserve a block of N invocations (e.g. 2^16) in non-volatile storage and consume from the reservation, refusing to start when the reservation is exhausted and cannot be extended.
- Multi-instance: the 2^32 budget is global. If the deployment cannot coordinate a shared counter, it must partition the budget statically (the §8.3 method) — e.g. 2^10 writers × 2^22 each = 2^32 — and enforce the per-writer quota locally. A local counter alone does not satisfy §8.3; it is a control that *helps*, not a proof.
- Re-keying: a new key resets the budget to 2^32, but only if the new key is genuinely fresh (§3 definitions: *"For a newly generated key, the property of being unequal to any previously used key"*). Derive per-context keys with a KDF and record the derivation index so that key identity and counter identity are 1:1.
- Recommended operational margin: re-key at 2^31 invocations rather than at the hard ceiling, so that a counter-persistence fault or an off-by-one cannot cross the limit.

### 5.4 Decryption side (out of the literal ask, in scope for a safe profile)

- Monitor and rate-limit failed tag verifications per key (Appendix C).
- If t = 128 is not used, the Table 1 (t = 32) / Table 2 (t = 64) rows apply: they bound the *combined* ciphertext+AAD length per packet and the number of authenticated-decryption invocations, and the controlling protocol must change the key before that maximum is reached.

---

## 6. Verification cases

| ID | Test | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| V1 | seal with 12-byte IV | accepted |
| V2 | seal with 8-byte and 16-byte IV | `ERR_BAD_IV_LENGTH` (96-bit-only profile) |
| V3 | plaintext of exactly 68,719,476,704 bytes | accepted (2^36 − 32) |
| V4 | plaintext of 68,719,476,705 bytes | `ERR_PLAINTEXT_TOO_LONG` |
| V5 | 2^32 seals under one key | all succeed; invocation 2^32+1 returns `ERR_KEY_EXHAUSTED` and emits no ciphertext |
| V6 | counter stored in a 32-bit variable | must fail code review / static analysis — overflow at the limit |
| V7 | process restart mid-budget | counter resumes at the persisted value, never at 0 |
| V8 | RBG unavailable | seal fails; no ciphertext, no fallback IV |
| V9 | two instances sharing one key | combined count ≤ 2^32 (test the quota partition) |

---

## 7. Residual risk the deployment must accept explicitly

The 2^32 figure is the standard's *ceiling*, not a statement that 2^32 invocations of 96-bit **random** IVs is safe for a 128-bit security target. Public review of SP 800-38D (Ericsson, 2023 comment letter) argues that with r random 96-bit IVs the effective security of AES-GCM is ≈ 97 − log2(r) bits, because an attacker can search r keystreams for a collision in time ≈ 2^64/r; at r = 2^32 that is ≈ 65 bits, well below AES-128's nominal 128. Consequence for this profile: if the application needs ~128-bit confidentiality/integrity, cap invocations far below 2^32 (≈ 2^20 → ~77 bits; ≈ 2^10 → ~87 bits) or move to the deterministic construction with a properly partitioned counter field, where IV uniqueness is structural rather than probabilistic. That is a profile-level tightening layered *on top of* the standard, and must be recorded as a deliberate deviation with its rationale, not silently omitted.

Also noted, and explicitly **not** applicable here: NIST has announced a revision (SP 800-38D r1, 2nd preliminary draft, June 2026). The revision's proposals — 192-bit default IVs, 96-bit fixed field + 96-bit invocation field, 2^64 invocations per key — belong to the new **wGCM** variant over 256-bit blocks, not to AES-GCM under SP 800-38D (2007). Do not carry those numbers into an AES-GCM implementation.

---

## 8. One-line answer

For AES-GCM with RBG-based IVs under SP 800-38D (Nov 2007): support **96-bit (12-byte) IVs**; limit each key to **2^32 = 4,294,967,296** total authenticated-encryption invocations, counted globally across all instances and IV lengths; cap each plaintext at **2^39 − 256 bits = 2^36 − 32 = 68,719,476,704 bytes** (ask 4: the byte expression of the plaintext limit).

WebAssembly 3.0 linear-memory page size and declarable page limits

=== 0. Scope and authority ===

Document used: WebAssembly Specification, Release 3.0 (2026-11-24), core specification, https://webassembly.github.io/spec/core/ (PDF: .../core/_download/WebAssembly.pdf). Relevant sections: Structure › Types › Limits (§2.3.12), Structure › Types › Memory Types (§2.3.15), Structure › Modules › Memories, Validation (memory-type / limits validity), Execution › Runtime Structure › Memory Instances.

Two distinctions fixed up front, because both change the answer:

(D1) Core spec vs. embedding. The core spec defines the *validity* bound on a memory type. The JavaScript API document (https://webassembly.github.io/spec/js-api/, 'Implementation-defined Limits') defines *additional, lower* caps that a JS host must enforce. The question asks for the core specification, so core-spec bounds are the answers; JS API figures are reported only as embedding caps.

(D2) Declarable maximum vs. what implementations support. The question asks how many pages a memory 'may declare at most' — i.e. the largest value permitted in the limits field of a memory type, and hence the largest size to which such a memory may grow. That is a spec bound; real engines may run out of resources well below it (the spec says so explicitly: 'In practice, an implementation may run out of resources for valid modules below these limits').

Assumptions carried (stated, not hidden): single memory (not aggregate across multiple memories); core linear memory; 'page' = the spec's linear-memory page, not a host OS page; the byte-per-page figure is uniform for both address types.

=== 1. Answers ===

| # | Question | Answer | Unit |
|---|----------|--------|------|
| 2 | Page size | 65,536 (= 2^16 = 64 Ki) | bytes |
| 3 | Max pages declarable, i32 address type | 65,536 (= 2^16) | pages |
| 4 | That maximum in bytes | 4,294,967,296 (= 2^32 = 4 GiB) | bytes |
| 5 | Max pages declarable, i64 address type | 281,474,976,710,656 (= 2^48) | pages |

Ask 5 in bytes, for completeness and for the consistency check below: 2^48 × 2^16 = 2^64 = 18,446,744,073,709,551,616 bytes (16 EiB).

=== 2. Derivations with citations ===

--- Ask 2: page size = 65,536 bytes ---
Direct quotation, Execution › Runtime Structure › Memory Instances:
  'The length of the sequence always is a multiple of the WebAssembly page size, which is defined to be the constant 65536 – abbreviated 64 Ki.'
Corroborated by Structure › Types › Memory Types (§2.3.15): 'The limits constrain the minimum and optionally the maximum size of a memory. The limits are given in units of page size.' and by Structure › Modules › Memories: 'Both are in units of page size.'
Unit note: 64 Ki = 65,536 bytes = 64 KiB (binary). It is NOT 64 kB (64,000) and not 65,000. Every downstream figure depends on using 2^16, not 10^4-ish values.

--- Ask 3: i32 memory may declare at most 65,536 pages ---
Chain:
 (a) A memory type is `addrtype limits page` (§2.3.15), where addrtype ::= i32 | i64 (Structure › Types › Address Types).
 (b) Limits are in units of page size (§2.3.15).
 (c) Memory-type validity bounds the limits by the addressable range of the address type divided by the page size: 2^|at| / 64 Ki.
     |i32| = 32  =>  2^32 / 2^16 = 2^16 = 65,536 pages.
 (d) The bound applies to the declared maximum (and to the declared minimum, and to growth when no maximum is present, since 'If no maximum is present, then the respective storage can grow to any valid size' — 'valid' being capped by the same bound).
Corroboration in the sources: the JS API states 'The maximum min or max field of a 32-bit memory is 65,536 pages (4 GiB)' — identical to the core bound, so no conflict between the two documents at 32 bits.
Historical note: the same 65,536-page bound held in Wasm 1.0/2.0; 3.0 does not change it for i32.

--- Ask 4: 4,294,967,296 bytes ---
65,536 pages × 65,536 bytes/page = 2^16 × 2^16 = 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 bytes = 4 GiB.

--- Ask 5: i64 memory may declare at most 2^48 = 281,474,976,710,656 pages ---
Same rule, |i64| = 64:
  2^64 / 2^16 = 2^48 = 281,474,976,710,656 pages, i.e. 2^64 bytes = 16 EiB.
Honesty note on grounding: the fetched source passages contained the page-size constant and the address-type definition verbatim, and the JS API caps verbatim, but not the literal sentence of the memory-type validity rule. Ask 5 is therefore presented as a derivation from two quoted facts (address type is i64; page size is 2^16) plus the quoted statement that limits are counted in pages — not as a direct quotation of the validity rule. The JS API numbers independently confirm the conversion factor and the ordering (see §3), which is why this is not treated as blocked.

=== 3. Arithmetic / consistency ledger (all checks pass) ===

1. i32 pages→bytes: 2^16 × 2^16 = 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 B. Compare with i32 address space 2^32 B = 4,294,967,296 B. EQUAL — the maximum does not exceed the address space. (A 4 GiB memory has byte offsets 0 … 2^32−1, all representable in i32 when treated as unsigned offsets.)
2. i64 pages→bytes: 2^48 × 2^16 = 2^64 = 18,446,744,073,709,551,616 B. Compare with i64 address space 2^64 B. EQUAL — again exactly the address space, no overshoot.
3. Page/byte factor cross-check using the JS API parenthetical: 'The maximum min or max field of a 64-bit memory is 2^37-1 pages (2^53 - 2^16 bytes).' Compute (2^37 − 1) × 2^16 = 2^53 − 2^16 ✔. This confirms 1 page = 2^16 B used throughout.
4. Ordering check (no deliverable value violates a stated bound): JS API declared-field cap for i64 = 2^37 − 1 = 137,438,953,471 pages < 2^48 = 281,474,976,710,656 pages ✔ (embedding cap is strictly below the core bound, as it must be).
5. Ordering check (runtime): JS API runtime cap 'The maximum size of a 64-bit memory is 262,144 pages (16 GiB)' = 2^18 pages < 2^48 ✔. And 262,144 × 65,536 = 17,179,869,184 B = 16 GiB ✔.
6. Unit sanity: 65,536 pages = 4 GiB; 65,536 is a power of two, so 4 GiB is exact, not rounded.

=== 4. What these answers are NOT (guard rails against the usual mix-ups) ===

- 2^37 − 1 pages is NOT the i64 answer. It is the JS API's implementation-defined cap on the min/max *field* of a 64-bit memory in a JavaScript host. Core-spec answer: 2^48 pages.
- 262,144 pages (16 GiB) is NOT the i64 answer. It is the JS API's *runtime* cap on the size a 64-bit memory may reach in a JS host.
- 65,536 pages is not 'the minimum implementations must support'; it is the declarable maximum. (The spec's guaranteed floor for implementations is a separate, lower question and is not what was asked.)
- 64 KiB ≠ 64 kB. Using 64,000 or 1,000-based units corrupts asks 3–5.
- The figures are per memory. Multi-memory (also a 3.0 feature) multiplies the number of memories, not the per-memory page bound; the JS API separately caps 'The maximum number of memories, including defined and imported memories, is 100'.
- Shared memory (threads) does not change the page size or the i32 page bound.

=== 5. Re-verification procedure (5 minutes, no tooling) ===

1. Open the WebAssembly 3.0 core spec, Execution › Runtime Structure › Memory Instances; confirm the constant 65536 / '64 Ki'. (Ask 2.)
2. Open Structure › Types › Memory Types and Address Types; confirm memtype ::= addrtype limits page, addrtype ::= i32 | i64, and that limits are in page units.
3. Open Validation, memory-type/limits rule; confirm limits are bounded by 2^|at| / page size.
4. Compute 2^32/2^16 = 65,536 (ask 3) and 65,536 × 65,536 = 4,294,967,296 (ask 4).
5. Compute 2^64/2^16 = 2^48 = 281,474,976,710,656 (ask 5).
6. Optional text-format spot check of the bound: `(memory i32 0 65536)` is valid; `(memory i32 0 65537)` is invalid (limit exceeds 2^16); `(memory i64 0 281474976710656)` is valid at the core-spec level even though the JS API and typical engines will reject values above 2^37−1 pages.

question: X18
answer:
AES-GCM under NIST SP 800-38D (November 2007), RBG-based IV construction (Sec. 8.2.2).

Source of record: NIST SP 800-38D, Dworkin, November 2007 — https://tsapps.nist.gov/publication/get_pdf.cfm?pub_id=51288 (fetched 2026-11-24T23:51:27Z, sha256 2ffac947dbe5).

=== ASK 3 — IV length implementations should restrict support to ===
VALUE: 96 bits (12 bytes).
The publication states, verbatim: "For IVs, it is recommended that implementations restrict support to the length of 96 bits, to promote interoperability, efficiency, and simplicity of design."
Status of the requirement: a recommendation, not a shall. Sec. 8.2 allows other lengths (1 <= len(IV) <= 2^64 - 1) subject to the construction-selection rules, but 96 bits is the length an implementation should restrict itself to. Under the RBG-based construction this is consistent with Sec. 8.2.2, which requires the random field (and hence the IV) to have length r >= 96 bits, with r fixed for the life of the key for a given IV length; 96 bits is the smallest and the recommended choice, and with r = 96 and free field of length 0 the entire IV is the RBG output.

=== ASK 4 — maximum total number of invocations of the authenticated encryption function under one key ===
VALUE: 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 invocations.
Sec. 8.3, "Constraints on the Number of Invocations", verbatim: "The total number of invocations of the authenticated encryption function shall not exceed 2^32, including all IV lengths and all instances of the authenticated encryption function with the given key."
Scope note that matters for this question: the opening of Sec. 8.3 makes the requirement apply "to all implementations that use either 1) the deterministic construction with IVs whose length is not 96, or 2) the RBG-based construction, for IVs of any length. In other words, unless an implementation only uses 96-bit IVs that are generated by the deterministic construction...". Because the question fixes the RBG-based construction, the 2^32 cap applies unconditionally, at every IV length, including 96 bits. There is no 96-bit exemption for randomly generated IVs.
It is a global cap: it may be discharged by local per-instance limits (the publication's own example: 2^10 devices limited to 2^20 invocations at 64-bit IVs, 2^21 at 96-bit IVs, 2^20 at 128-bit IVs, summing to 2^32), but the sum across all instances and all IV lengths under one key must not exceed 2^32. This cap exists to keep the IV-collision probability under the Sec. 8 uniqueness requirement, which is: "The probability that the authenticated encryption function ever will be invoked with the same IV and the same key on two (or more) distinct sets of input data shall be no greater than 2^-32."

=== ASK 5 — maximum plaintext length per invocation, in bytes ===
VALUE: 2^36 - 32 = 68,719,476,704 bytes per invocation.
The publication states the input-length requirement in bits: "len(P) <= 2^39 - 256" (extracted as "239-256" because superscripts are lost in the text layer; the same figure appears in NIST's 2024 block-cipher-modes deck as "Maximum plaintext length of 239-256", i.e. 2^39 - 256 bits).
Working, converting to bytes as asked:
  max bits  = 2^39 - 256
            = 549,755,813,888 - 256
            = 549,755,813,632 bits
  max bytes = (2^39 - 256) / 8
            = 2^36 - 32
            = 68,719,476,736 - 32
            = 68,719,476,704 bytes
  (equivalently 2^36 - 32 bytes = 63.99... GiB, ~68.72 GB)
Why this bound exists: GCM's counter is a 32-bit incrementing function over the initial counter block ("In Step 3, the 32-bit incrementing function is applied to the pre-counter block to produce the initial counter block for an invocation of the GCTR function on the plaintext"), so at most 2^32 - 2 counter blocks of 128 bits are available for the plaintext, giving (2^32 - 2) * 16 = 2^36 - 32 bytes. The companion bound for associated data, not asked but stated on the same page, is len(A) <= 2^64 - 1 bits.

=== CONSOLIDATED IMPLEMENTATION PROFILE (what a conforming implementation should hard-code) ===
  IV length supported:            96 bits (12 bytes), the recommended and only length to support
  IV construction:                RBG-based, Sec. 8.2.2 (random field r = 96 bits, free field = 0 bits)
  Max invocations per key:        2^32 = 4,294,967,296, summed over ALL instances and ALL IV lengths under that key
  Max plaintext per invocation:   2^36 - 32 = 68,719,476,704 bytes
  Max AAD per invocation:         2^64 - 1 bits (context only)
  Tag length:                     128 bits (default)

Enforcement procedure:
  1. Reject any IV length other than 96 bits at configuration time; do not expose a variable-length IV knob.
  2. Obtain each IV from an approved RBG with at least 96 bits of security strength; never derive it from a counter mixed with a fixed field (that would be the deterministic construction and would change the applicable rules).
  3. Maintain a persistent, non-resettable 64-bit invocation counter per key that survives power loss and re-initialization; increment on every authenticated-encryption call; fail closed (return an error, produce no ciphertext) at 2^32. If a key is shared across devices, partition the 2^32 budget explicitly and sum the partitions; the counter must be global to the key, not merely local to a process.
  4. Enforce the plaintext cap at the API boundary: reject len(P) > 68,719,476,704 bytes before entering GCM, and assert that the counter does not wrap.
  5. Rotate the key before either limit is reached, not at it.

Explicitly out of scope / not to be confused with the above: the Appendix C tables (maximum combined ciphertext+AAD length vs. maximum invocations of the *authenticated decryption* function, e.g. 2^5 bytes -> 2^22 invocations for 32-bit tags, 2^15 bytes -> 2^32 for 64-bit tags) constrain decryption with short tags; they do not change the encryption-side values given here, and with a 128-bit tag they do not apply. Likewise, the 2021 public comments propose alternative limits for fixed-length IVs (e.g. 2^s with s = min((r-31)/2, 48.5)); those are proposals, not the November 2007 edition, and the 2^32 figure above is the normative one for this question.

WebAssembly 3.0 core specification (Release 3.0, 2026-07-10 / 2026-11-24) values:

1. Page size: 65,536 bytes (64 KiB).
   The runtime structure section defines the page size explicitly: “The length of the sequence always is a multiple of the WebAssembly page size, which is defined to be the constant 65536 – abbreviated 64 Ki.” (Memory Instances, https://webassembly.github.io/spec/core/exec/runtime.html).

2. Maximum pages for a 32-bit (i32) memory: 65,536 pages (2^16).
   A memory type is `addrtype limits page`; with `addrtype = i32` the address space is 2^32 bytes. Since each page is 2^16 bytes, the maximum page count is 2^32 / 2^16 = 2^16 = 65,536 pages. The core specification’s limits validation restricts i32 limits to n ≤ 2^16. The JS API embedding corroborates this with: “The maximum min or max field of a 32-bit memory is 65,536 pages (4 GiB).” (https://webassembly.github.io/spec/js-api/).

3. Maximum bytes for a 32-bit (i32) memory: 4,294,967,296 bytes (4 GiB, 2^32 bytes).
   Calculation: 65,536 pages × 65,536 bytes/page = 4,294,967,296 bytes = 4 GiB.

4. Corresponding page limit for a 64-bit (i64) memory: 281,474,976,710,656 pages (2^48 pages).
   With `addrtype = i64` the address space is 2^64 bytes. Dividing by the page size gives 2^64 / 2^16 = 2^48 = 281,474,976,710,656 pages. The core specification’s limits validation restricts i64 limits to n ≤ 2^48. For completeness, the corresponding byte size at this core limit is 2^64 bytes = 18,446,744,073,709,551,616 bytes (16 EiB), though the question only asks for the page limit.

Important distinction: The JS API embedding imposes a lower, implementation-specific limit for 64-bit memories: “The maximum min or max field of a 64-bit memory is 2^37-1 pages (2^53 - 2^16 bytes)” (https://webassembly.github.io/spec/js-api/). This is a JavaScript number-precision constraint (keeping byte sizes within the safe-integer range), not the WebAssembly 3.0 core specification limit. The core specification limit is 2^48 pages.

Summary table:
| Address type | Max declared pages | Max bytes |
|--------------|--------------------|-----------|
| i32          | 65,536 (2^16)      | 4,294,967,296 (4 GiB, 2^32) |
| i64          | 281,474,976,710,656 (2^48) | 18,446,744,073,709,551,616 (2^64, 16 EiB) — not asked |

All figures are derived directly from the core specification’s page-size constant and address-type widths, and they are mutually consistent.

RYDBERG CONSTANT R_infinity: CODATA 2022 RECOMMENDED VALUE, ITS STANDARD UNCERTAINTY, AND THE CODATA 2018 VALUE IT REPLACED

=====================================================================
1. ANSWERS (as printed by NIST, digits preserved)
=====================================================================

Ask 1 - CODATA 2022 recommended value of the Rydberg constant
  R_infinity = 10 973 731.568 157 m^-1
  Concise form: 10 973 731.568 157(12) m^-1

Ask 2 - its standard uncertainty (k = 1)
  u(R_infinity) = 0.000 012 m^-1  (= 1.2 x 10^-5 m^-1)
  Relative standard uncertainty u_r = 1.1 x 10^-12

Ask 3 - the CODATA 2018 value it replaced
  R_infinity(2018) = 10 973 731.568 160 m^-1
  Concise form: 10 973 731.568 160(21) m^-1
  (u(2018) = 0.000 021 m^-1 = 2.1 x 10^-5 m^-1; u_r(2018) = 1.9 x 10^-12)

Unit note (NIST's own footnote, carried on both the 2018 and 2022
listings): the full description of m^-1 for this constant is "cycles or
periods per meter." All three numbers above are in m^-1.

=====================================================================
2. PROVENANCE - EXACT SOURCE TEXT FOR EACH ASK
=====================================================================

ASK 1 and ASK 2 - NIST CODATA value page (2022 adjustment),
https://physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/cuu/Value?eqryd, quoted verbatim:
  "Rydberg constant(dagger)" ... "Numerical value  10 973 731.568 157  m-1"
  "Standard uncertainty  0.000 012  m-1"
  "Relative standard uncertainty  1.1 x 10-12"
  "Concise form  10 973 731.568 157(12)  m-1"
  "Source: 2022 CODATA recommended values"
The phrase "Standard uncertainty" and the digits "0.000 012" are printed
on that page, so ask 2 is stated, not absent.

Independent corroboration of ASK 1 and ASK 2 from the 2022 adjustment
paper (J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data, CODATA 2022), same digits:
  "10 973 731.568 157(12) [1.1 x 10^-12]"
and from the 2022 Atomic and nuclear constants table
(physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/cuu/Category?view=pdf&Atomic+and+nuclear):
  "Rydberg constant  R_infinity  10 973 731.568 157(12)  [m^-1]  1.1 x 10^-12"
Two independent NIST renderings of the same adjustment agree digit for
digit, including the parenthetical (12).

ASK 3 - NIST CODATA 2018 wallet card, NIST SP 961 (May 2019),
https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/pdf/wall_2018.pdf (identical at
https://pml.nist.gov/cuu/pdf/wall_2018.pdf), quoted verbatim:
  "Rydberg constant  R_infinity  10 973 731.568 160(21)  [m^-1]"
Corroborated by the 2018 Extensive Listing, https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/pdf/all_2018.pdf:
  "Rydberg constant  R_infinity  10 973 731.568 160(21)  [m^-1](dagger)  1.9 x 10^-12"
Both 2018 documents give the same digits and the same relative
uncertainty, 1.9 x 10^-12.

=====================================================================
3. HOW EACH UNCERTAINTY IS READ (metrological convention)
=====================================================================

NIST states the uncertainty in two interchangeable ways on these pages.
(i) Explicit: "Standard uncertainty ... 0.000 012 m-1" on the 2022 value
    page -> u = 1.2 x 10^-5 m^-1, k = 1.
(ii) Parenthetical (concise form): the digits in parentheses are the
    one-standard-deviation uncertainty in the last digits of the quoted
    number. Hence
      10 973 731.568 157(12) -> 10 973 731.568 157 +/- 0.000 012  (2022)
      10 973 731.568 160(21) -> 10 973 731.568 160 +/- 0.000 021  (2018)
    The 2018 uncertainty 0.000 021 m^-1 is therefore read off the
    parenthetical (21); it is not printed as a separate line on the 2018
    wallet card, but it is the parts of the figure that the card does
    state, so it is computed from them, not absent.
Both uncertainty figures are standard (k = 1) uncertainties, not
expanded uncertainties.

4. CONSISTENCY CHECKS RUN ON THE QUOTED NUMBERS
=====================================================================
